il_articles.contenu:
Summary

OPEC+ held November oil output targets steady on Sunday, but its seven core members are still pumping about 5 million bpd below prewar levels because of the Iran war, while a capacity review key to 2027 quotas has slipped to mid-November.

The rollover keeps the supply picture unchanged, and that picture is tight. Brent is still above $100 a barrel, up from about $73 before the war began in late February. Friday's dip on Europe's agreement to release diesel reserves at Washington's request looks like relief, not a turn in the trend. With physical barrels constrained by war-related export disruption rather than by policy, OPEC+ ceilings have little near-term pricing power. Traders are watching Hormuz flows and Gulf export data more closely than quota headlines. The delayed capacity review also leaves the 2027 supply path uncertain. That keeps a risk premium on longer-dated contracts and raises the chance of quota disputes once flows normalise.

OPEC+ can set any targets it likes, but the Iran war, not the quota table, still decides how much oil it actually pumps.

Seven core OPEC+ members kept November production targets unchanged at a brief online meeting on Sunday, as expected.

Gulf exports have run at 60% to 80% of normal in recent months because of war-related disruption. Core output was about 25 million bpd in August, roughly 5 million bpd below February's prewar level.

A capacity review central to setting 2027 quotas has slipped from end-September to mid-November, sources said. Not all members have submitted data.

The consultant's report is due in mid-November, in time for a group-wide meeting in late November. The core members meet next on November 1.

About 2 million bpd of cuts remain in place, and sources say output changes are unlikely before 2027.

OPEC+ agreed on Sunday to keep its oil production targets unchanged for November, Reuters reported. The decision was widely expected and does little to change the reality on the ground: Gulf producers are still pumping far below their quotas because of the US-Israeli war on Iran.

The decision was taken in a short online meeting of the group's seven core members: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman. Export disruptions linked to the conflict have left Gulf exports running at between 60% and 80% of normal levels in recent months.

UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said the unchanged ceilings matched expectations. He noted that output remains well short of quota despite rising flows through the Strait of Hormuz, which leaves the oil market tight.

OPEC data show the seven core members produced about 25 million barrels per day in August. That was more than 600,000 bpd higher than July but still roughly 5 million bpd below February's prewar levels. The group has raised targets for much of 2026 after years of cuts, yet most of those increases have existed only on paper.

The war has also delayed a review that is central to setting members' 2027 quotas. OPEC+ ordered the assessment of each member's maximum sustainable production capacity in late 2025, with completion due by the end of September. Two sources toldReuterson Friday that the deadline has slipped to mid-November. The conflict has held up capacity expansion projects across the Middle East and made estimates of future output potential uncertain. Not all members have submitted the required data, the sources said.

US consultant DeGolyer and MacNaughton is assessing all members except Russia, Iran and Venezuela, which are under US sanctions. It is now expected to deliver its report in mid-November. That would still allow ministers to consider the findings at a group-wide meeting in late November.

The exercise is politically sensitive. Members with lower assessed capacity could face pressure to accept smaller quotas, while those that have expanded may push for more. The United Arab Emirates, which sought a higher quota to reflect its growing capacity, left the alliance in May. Iraq has also pressed for a larger allocation.

OPEC+ still has about 2 million bpd of cuts in place across most members, and sources have said changes to output are unlikely before 2027. The seven core members meet next on November 1.
il_articles.titre: Weekend: OPEC+ holds November output steady with core members 5 million bpd below prewar levels

il_articles.contenu:
Summary

France's bond premium has moved above Italy's as debt, weak growth and political uncertainty worry investors. What it could mean for EUR/USD, Europe and the CAC 40, which has broken a multi-year rising support trend, but the more concerning development is what has happened afterward: buyers have so far shown little urgency to defend the break.

France is becoming Europe’s new fiscal stress test: what it means for bonds, EUR/USD and the CAC 40

France is no longer being treated by markets as an unquestionably "core" European sovereign. The clearest warning is coming from government bonds: investors are demanding a larger premium to lend to France than to Italy. That does not mean a French debt crisis is inevitable, but if the trend continues, the consequences could reach the euro, European banks and French equities.

For traders and investors, the important point is not simply that French borrowing costs have risen. It is thatFrance is being repriced relative to the rest of Europe.

The bond market is sending a message about France

Vanguard, one of the world's largest asset managers, has added considerable weight to the debate. The Financial Times recently reported that Vanguard sees France as a"degrading credit", pointing to persistent deficits, political uncertainty and the prospect of still higher borrowing costs. Vanguard had already said in its 2026 outlook that France was the euro-area fiscal situation causing it the most concern.Financial Times

But Vanguard's opinion is not actually the most important signal.

The bond market itself is.

Germany's 10-year Bund is generally treated as the benchmark sovereign bond for the euro area. Investors therefore often measure another euro-area government's perceived risk by asking how much more yield they demand to hold its debt instead of German debt.

One basis point is 0.01 percentage point. So a French-German spread of 130 basis points means France must offer roughly1.30 percentage points more yield than Germanyat the 10-year maturity.

That premium has risen dramatically.

Around September 24, the French 10-year spread over Germany was approximately110 basis points, while comparable Italian risk premiums were around the low-90s. By October 1, the French spread had moved to roughly 130 basis points, and Reuters reported that it subsequently pushed beyond 140 basis points, around levels not seen since the euro-area debt crisis in 2012. Italy's spread also widened during the global bond selloff, but remained below France's.Idéal Investisseur

That reversal deserves attention.

For years, Italy was the country routinely associated with high debt and elevated sovereign risk. Today, investors are demandingmore compensation for holding French debt than Italian debt.

One important clarification: this doesnotmean Italy is "15% safer" than France. Sovereign spreads are prices, not direct probabilities of default. What they do show is how much additional yield the market currently demands for taking one country's sovereign risk rather than another's.

What the CAC 40 chart is showing

The important development is not simply that the CAC 40 has broken its long-term rising support line. It is thatthe break has so far failed to attract the kind of buying response that previously appeared around this trend.

Earlier tests of the long-term trendline produced visible rejection and relatively quick recovery. This latest move looks different. Price has slipped below the rising support after already losing the shorter-term ascending channel, and the response beneath the trendline has been relatively subdued. In other words, buyers are not yet treating the break as an obvious opportunity.

That changes the interpretation of the trendline. For several years it acted as an area where weakness was absorbed. Once price moves underneath such a structure, the key question becomes whether the marketquickly reclaims itor begins accepting prices below it.

What to watch next

A relatively fast recovery back above the broken trendline, particularly if followed by stronger weekly closes, would make this look more like afailed breakdownand suggest buyers are returning.

But if the CAC 40 continues trading beneath the line and rebounds repeatedly stall around the former support area, the technical message becomes materially more bearish. The old support could then start behaving as resistance.

The absence of aggressive dip-buying is therefore arguablymore important than the initial break itself.

Educational takeaway

Major trendlines are not powerful because price mathematically "must" bounce from them. Their value comes from observinghow market participants react around them. When a support level that repeatedly attracted buyers suddenly stops doing so, that change in behavior can carry more information than the line itself.

Why investors are becoming more worried about France

The concern is not based on one disappointing economic release.

It is the interaction between debt, weak growth, political constraints and rising refinancing costs.

France's public debt reached approximately119% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, while the government expects a deficit of about5.4% of GDP this year. The European Commission had already projected debt moving above 120% of GDP in 2027. France also plans to issue a record€340 billion of medium- and long-term debt in 2027, just as older bonds issued at much lower interest rates increasingly need to be refinanced.Reuters

That last point matters.

A government does not suddenly refinance its entire debt pile at today's interest rate. But as old low-cost bonds mature and are replaced with much more expensive debt, the interest bill gradually rises. Higher interest costs then consume more of the budget, making it harder to reduce the deficit without either raising revenue or cutting spending.

The economic backdrop is not providing much help.

Official INSEE data show that French GDPcontracted 0.2% in the first quarter and was flat in the second quarter of 2026. Household purchasing power per consumption unit fell another 0.6% in Q2.Insee

The labor market is also softening. France's unemployment rate reached8.3% in Q2, up 0.7 percentage point from a year earlier, while private payroll employment recorded itssixth consecutive quarter of year-on-year decline.Insee

Weak growthmakes reducing the deficit harder.

Fiscal tighteningcan weigh further on growth.

Political resistancemakes tightening difficult to implement.

Higher bond yieldsthen increase the cost of waiting.

The government's proposed 2027 budget attempts to break that loop through around€54 billion of savings and revenue measures, but the package faces a divided parliament and substantial domestic opposition.Reuters

Why this could become a European problem, not just a French one

France is simply too large for markets to treat sustained sovereign stress as a local curiosity.

The danger is not necessarily a dramatic default scenario. A much more realistic transmission mechanism isprogressively tighter financial conditions.

Higher French government yields can feed into corporate borrowing costs, bank funding, mortgages and asset valuations. If investors begin demanding larger risk premiums from other fiscally vulnerable euro-area countries at the same time, the problem starts moving from French fiscal policy toward euro-area financial fragmentation.

That is when the European Central Bank becomes important.

The ECB does have a tool, the Transmission Protection Instrument, designed to counter unjustified and disorderly widening in sovereign spreads. But Reuters reported that intervention on France's behalf currently appears difficult to justify because much of the repricing reflects genuine fiscal concerns, the movement has so far remained relatively orderly, and France is already subject to the EU's excessive-deficit procedure.Reuters

That distinction matters to traders.

The ECB may eventually act againstcontagion.

It is much less straightforward for the ECB to protect a government from higher borrowing costs when investors are responding rationally to deteriorating fiscal fundamentals.

What does the France story mean for EUR/USD?

One tempting interpretation would be that higher French yields should support the euro because investors can earn more interest.

That misses the nature of the move.

There is a major difference between yields rising because an economy is strong and yields rising because investors demand alarger sovereign-risk premium.

The latter can be bearish for the currency.

That is what markets have recently been showing. As French-German spreads widened beyond 140 basis points, investors sold the euro. Reuters reported that EUR/USD fell below1.1215 on October 1, while the euro also weakened sharply against the Swiss franc as investors reduced European risk exposure.Reuters

France is not the only variable affecting EUR/USD. The US yield advantage, Federal Reserve expectations, oil prices, European inflation and broader dollar demand may be even more important on a given day.

But French sovereign stress adds another potential bearish channel.

France deteriorates further

If French spreads continue widening, French assets underperform and concerns spread into other euro-area sovereigns, the euro would have another fundamental headwind.

France stabilizes

If the budget process becomes more credible and the French-German spread begins sustainably retracing its recent surge, one source of pressure on the euro would be removed.

This fits the broader relationship between currencies and relative bond yields explained in investingLive's guide toforex and yield spreads.

Is shorting the CAC 40 the obvious France trade?

Not necessarily.

The CAC 40 fell1.6% on October 1as French bond yields surged and investors assessed the government's austerity budget. French financial shares have been particularly sensitive to the deterioration in sovereign sentiment.Reuters

That creates a legitimate bearish thesis if French financial conditions continue deteriorating.

But there is an important complication:the CAC 40 is not a pure bet on the French domestic economy.

Many of its largest companies generate substantial revenues outside France. A weaker euro can even improve the translated earnings of some internationally exposed companies. Luxury, industrial and multinational businesses may therefore behave very differently from French banks or companies primarily exposed to domestic demand.

So a trader considering bearish exposure should first ask what exactly the thesis is.

If the thesis is French sovereign stress:French banks and other rate-sensitive domestic exposures may react more directly.

If the thesis is broad French equity underperformance:the CAC 40 becomes more relevant, particularly if it begins consistently lagging indices such as Germany's DAX or the broader STOXX Europe 600.

If global equities continue rising strongly:simply shorting the CAC because France has fiscal problems may be a poor expression of the idea. International earnings and global risk appetite can overwhelm domestic weakness.

Without an actual price setup, entry, invalidation and risk plan, this should be treated as amarket thesis to monitor rather than a completed short trade.

What would tell us that the France problem is getting worse?

The best confirmation may continue to come from bonds rather than newspaper headlines.

French-German sovereign spread:Continued widening from already elevated levels would show investors demanding still more compensation for French risk.

France versus Italy:If France continues trading with a persistently larger premium than Italy, the change in Europe's traditional sovereign-risk hierarchy becomes harder to dismiss as temporary noise.

French banks and CAC 40 relative performance:Further underperformance, particularly while other European markets remain stable, would suggest that the fiscal issue is increasingly being priced into equities.

EUR/USD and EUR/CHF:Sustained euro weakness alongside wider French spreads would show the stress extending beyond France itself.

French debt auctions:France needs enormous amounts of financing. Investor demand and the yields required at future auctions therefore become increasingly important.

The opposite would matter just as much. A credible budget compromise, orderly debt auctions and a meaningful narrowing of the French-German spread would argue that markets had already priced a substantial amount of bad news.

The bigger signal investors should not ignore

Vanguard's warning matters because it shows that a major long-term asset manager is treating France's fiscal trajectory seriously.

But the more important development is thatinvestors are already voting with prices.

France's borrowing premium has moved above Italy's, its 10-year borrowing costs have risen toward levels not seen for decades, and political difficulty is colliding with weak growth precisely when the government needs to convince investors that debt can eventually be stabilized.

That does not make France the next euro crisis automatically.

It does make France one of the most important macro risks in Europe to monitor.

For EUR/USD traders, French spreads have become another piece of the euro's fundamental puzzle. For European equity traders, French banks and relative CAC 40 performance may provide an earlier signal than the index headline itself.

And for longer-term investors, the key question is no longer whether France has a large debt burden. That is already known.

The question is whether financial markets are beginning to demand a permanently higher price for financing it.

For additional background, investingLive recently examined how rising sovereign yields are affecting France, Italy and other developed markets in itsguide to the global bond selloff.

il_articles.titre: All B-1 bombers returning to U.S. from U.K. base (not what you think)
il_articles.contenu:
Summary

The US has pulled all its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford in England over security concerns, after six suspects were arrested over a foiled plot against the base that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said bore strong indications of an Iranian role.

For oil, the move is a reminder that the Iran conflict now reaches allied military infrastructure in Europe. That keeps geopolitical risk elevated in crude pricing even with no direct supply disruption. Relocating the bombers to the continental US doesn't reduce Washington's strike capacity, so traders are unlikely to read it as de-escalation. Any firmer evidence of direct Iranian state involvement in a plot on British soil could raise the risk premium further. It could also prompt questions about Western retaliation and the security of energy shipping routes. The muted, uncertain UK assessment may limit the immediate reaction, but it leaves a headline risk hanging over the oil complex.

A suspected Iran-linked plot against a British air base has pushed Washington to fly its Iran bomber missions from home, showing how far the conflict's reach now extends.

The US has withdrawn all B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, northwest of London, citing security concerns over suspected plots against the base.

About a dozen B-1s had been stationed there, and Fairford had served as a hub for US bomber strikes on Iran.

The Pentagon said the aircraft have returned to home stations in the US and remain ready for global strike missions. Britain's Ministry of Defence declined to comment.

Six suspects were arrested over a foiled attack on the base and later released on bail. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham cited strong indications of Iranian involvement.

A senior US official said a branch of Iran's Revolutionary Guard recruited UK nationals for a multi-step plot that included a local diversion.

Some UK officials question how sophisticated the planned attack was, and the British investigation is ongoing.

The United States has withdrawn all of its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford, the British air base northwest of London, because of security concerns linked to suspected plots against the facility. The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported the move on Sunday, citing American officials.

The move marks a notable shift for Washington, which has used the base as a hub for launching bomber strikes on Iran. Around a dozen B-1s had been stationed at Fairford before their recent departure.

In a statement, the Pentagon said operational security had prevented it from confirming the aircraft movements as they happened. It acknowledged that every US bomber deployed to Fairford had now returned to its home station in the United States. The department added that the aircraft remained ready to carry out global strike missions from the continental US. Britain's Ministry of Defence declined to comment.

The withdrawal follows the arrest of six people in connection with what US and British officials described as an attack on the base that was foiled the previous Sunday. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were strong indications that Iran had played a role. The case has remained murky, with British authorities releasing the suspects on bail while their investigation continues.

According to the Journal, US officials were aware of an Iran-linked plan to attack the bombers and kill personnel at Fairford. A senior US official said a branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps had recruited UK nationals to carry out the scheme. The plan involved several steps, including a diversion in the surrounding neighbourhood.

British authorities, however, are still trying to establish exactly what happened. Some UK officials have questioned how sophisticated the planned attack really was. That gap between the confident US account and the more cautious British view leaves key questions open, including the extent of direct Iranian involvement and how advanced the plot had become.

The practical upshot is that any further US bomber operations against Iran look set to be flown from American soil rather than a forward base in Europe. The Pentagon insists its global strike capability remains in place. More broadly, the episode suggests the reach of the Iran conflict now extends to allied military infrastructure in Europe. Defence planners, and energy markets, are likely to watch that closely as the British investigation unfolds.
